lists.text:
1. Require weekly curbside collection of food scraps and other organics for every household in the city.
2. Provide households with free compostable bags or durable reusable caddies for collecting food scraps.
3. Install clearly labeled food-waste drop-off bins at every park, plaza, and major transit stop.
4. Equip public markets with staffed collection points where vendors can deliver unsold edible produce.
5. Build a municipal composting facility that turns food scraps and yard trimmings into usable soil amendment.
6. Launch special pickups for frozen food during heat waves, when power outages cause widespread freezer spoilage.
7. Require grocery stores to separate and donate edible surplus before it reaches the waste stream.
8. Waive or discount business license fees for restaurants that document food donation or composting.
9. Impose fines on businesses that discard edible food into dumpsters rather than donating it.
10. Create a citywide "rescue" app where surplus food is posted in real time for pickup.
11. Require delivery platforms to redirect unclaimed orders to food banks instead of discarding them.
12. Change platform rules so drivers can return orders flagged as surplus rather than disposing of them.
13. Offer "use it up" cooking classes through libraries and recreation centers.
14. Run a citywide campaign encouraging households to inventory their refrigerator and pantry regularly.
15. Distribute date-label stickers that clearly distinguish "best before" from "use by" dates.
16. Publish plain-language guidance on how to tell food that is safe to eat from food that is not.
17. Provide refrigerator and freezer repair vouchers for low-income households and seniors.
18. Establish a network of community refrigerators in neighborhoods with high food insecurity.
19. Install smart meters in commercial kitchens to track production levels and identify over-preparation.
20. Offer small businesses free food-waste audits and customized reduction plans.
21. Require large food waste generators to keep waste logs and report their diversion rates annually.
22. Set a citywide food waste reduction target and report progress publicly each year.
23. Weigh food waste at transfer stations to measure tonnage by source and route.
24. Publish a public dashboard showing which neighborhoods and business categories waste the most food.
25. Offer curbside organics collection for residents who lack outdoor space or cannot compost.
26. Supply shared compost containers to apartment complexes that cannot host individual bins.
27. Co-locate organics bins at apartment buildings with multilingual signage to improve use.
28. Create a food-pantry aggregator system to reduce duplicate collections and spoiled duplicate stock.
29. Permit restaurants to offer safe "doggy bag" leftovers for pet food where regulation allows.
30. Provide leftover-safe meal planning resources through clinics, schools, and social service agencies.
31. Launch a "buy less, save more" campaign promoting smaller default portions and package sizes.
32. Require food-service establishments to offer half portions and smaller sides as standard options.
33. Encourage supermarkets to discount ripe produce and items nearing expiration.
34. Adopt a citywide markdown policy requiring stores to lower prices on products approaching spoilage.
35. Support flash discounts at bakeries, cafes, and delis for end-of-day unsold items.
36. Set a standard for "rescue shelves" in grocery stores where discounted surplus is displayed.
37. Partner with local farms to sell "ugly vegetable" boxes at reduced prices.
38. Offer produce box subscriptions sized to actual household consumption levels.
39. Establish a shared community freezer and pantry in each district of the city.
40. Teach residents food preservation skills such as freezing, pickling, drying, and fermenting.
41. Run seasonal preservation workshops so residents can process surplus during peak harvest months.
42. Organize neighborhood food-sharing swaps for homemade preserves and garden surplus.
43. Build a citywide leftover recipe website built around seasonal, low-cost ingredients.
44. Encourage restaurants to donate prepared surplus through contracted food recovery organizations.
45. Train food recovery groups in safe handling, repackaging, and distribution of surplus food.
46. Offer cold storage space to small food recovery organizations that lack refrigeration.
47. Provide insulated transport boxes so volunteers can deliver donated food without spoilage.
48. Recruit and background-check volunteers as "food rescue drivers" for pickup routes.
49. Use city fleet vehicles during off-peak hours to collect surplus donations from businesses.
50. Provide per-pound grants to food recovery organizations for every pound of food rescued.
51. Require catering companies to plan portions based on confirmed guest counts.
52. Require event organizers to offer smaller portions and seconds lines at buffets.
53. Restrict large buffets and catered events that consistently leave excess food.
54. Streamline health certifications so restaurants can donate surplus without lengthy delays.
55. Simplify tax documentation for small donors so completing a donation is not burdensome.
56. Offer tax credits to restaurants and supermarkets for verified food donations.
57. Recognize businesses, schools, and neighborhoods with annual "waste-less hero" awards.
58. Include food waste reduction requirements in city procurement contracts and vendor contracts.
59. Require city cafeterias, schools, and offices to donate safe surplus food.
60. Incorporate food waste education and portion estimation into school curricula.
61. Start school compost clubs that weigh lunch leftovers and track trends over time.
62. Hold competitions among schools to identify the lowest per-student food waste levels.
63. Redesign cafeteria lines and signage to encourage students to take only what they will eat.
64. Offer pre-ordering and selectable portions in school lunches to cut plate waste.
65. Require farmers market vendors to post storage and ripeness guidance for their produce.
66. Arrange donations of surplus from city-supported farmers markets to nearby food pantries.
67. Run "glut" campaigns at community gardens that convert peak-season surplus into preserved goods for pantries.
68. Coordinate grocery store donation schedules with food bank operating hours to avoid rejected deliveries.
69. Build neighborhood food hubs that combine collection, storage, and distribution in one accessible site.
70. Contract postal and courier services to move surplus food cheaply across the city.
71. Create a "spoilage alert" system that texts households about foods at immediate risk of rotting.
72. Provide home composting starter kits and instruction guides to households in dense neighborhoods.
73. Install shared compost lockers or sealed chute systems in multi-unit residential buildings.
74. Develop markets for surplus animal feed, spent brewery grain, and other safe organic byproducts.
75. Partner with animal shelters, farms, and rescues to divert appropriate food scraps.
76. Support rendering and anaerobic digestion facilities to handle food-processing byproducts.
77. Add anaerobic digestion at the wastewater treatment plant to turn organics into energy.
78. Require commercial waste haulers to report where they deliver food waste, preventing illegal dumping.
79. Ban edible food from landfill disposal for large businesses, with narrow documented exceptions.
80. Phase in a full ban on landfilling food waste for all generators over several years.
81. Adjust waste fees so that disposal costs more than donation, composting, or digestion.
82. Provide free composting service and collection containers to small restaurants.
83. Create a fast-track permit process for new food donation and recovery enterprises.
84. Award small grants for cold storage, shelving, and safe packaging to community groups.
85. Produce translated donation and food safety guidelines for the city's diverse communities.
86. Develop culturally appropriate recipes and preservation guides to reduce waste of familiar foods.
87. Work with community organizations to deliver hands-on food waste education to underserved neighborhoods.
88. Partner with utilities to offer time-of-day pricing that rewards efficient refrigerator and freezer use.
89. Create a lending library of food tools such as dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and blender blenders.
90. Run a public awareness campaign showing the environmental and financial cost of wasted food.
91. Use city advertising spaces, bus shelters, and transit screens to promote "eat it, share it, compost it" messages.
92. Staff a city food waste hotline where residents can request collection or get advice.
93. Train sanitation workers to recognize and report patterns of commercial food dumping.
94. Use anonymized data from smart bins to target outreach where waste is heaviest.
95. Hold an annual citywide food waste reduction week with demonstrations, contests, and prizes.
96. Embed food waste reduction targets in the city's climate action plan and budget.
97. Require new developments to include dedicated food waste storage, collection, and composting space.
98. Celebrate and directly fund businesses that meet ambitious food waste reduction benchmarks.
99. Commission independent annual audits of the city's food waste programs and publish the findings.
100. Survey residents and businesses each year to measure attitudes, identify barriers, and guide the next round of policies.

lists.text:
1. Expand curbside collection of food scraps and yard waste to every household, with separate bins for compostable organics.
2. Offer free kitchen compost caddies and counter-top composters to households that enroll in the organics program.
3. Place clearly marked neighborhood compost drop-off points in parks, apartment complexes, and community centers.
4. Build a municipal composting facility that turns collected organics into compost for parks, schools, and gardens.
5. Develop an anaerobic digestion facility that converts food scraps and wastewater sludge into biogas and soil amendments.
6. Give residents free bags of finished compost or vouchers for bulk compost at neighborhood collection sites.
7. Require restaurants and institutional kitchens to separate food scraps from trash and deliver them to processors.
8. Provide grocery stores with standardized color-coded containers for spoiled produce, expired dairy, and other organics.
9. Print multilingual instructions on compostable bags to reduce plastic contamination in organics streams.
10. Use friendly contamination audits and feedback to teach composters how to keep unwanted materials out of their bins.
11. Offer rebates for reusable or certified compostable liners so households do not use plastic bags for organics.
12. Permit small businesses to join curbside organics pickups at affordable commercial rates.
13. Create a city food-rescue coordination hub that matches donors, charities, and volunteers in real time.
14. Launch a mobile app that alerts volunteers when supermarkets, restaurants, and markets have surplus food available.
15. Provide tax credits or fee reductions to businesses that donate safe, unopened surplus food.
16. Offer grants to food banks, shelters, and nonprofits to expand their cold storage and rescue capacity.
17. Clarify liability protections so restaurants and grocers can donate food without fear of legal risk.
18. Require large food retailers and food-service businesses to maintain written surplus-management and donation policies.
19. Establish “rescue boxes” where stores assemble discounted bags of safe, soon-to-be-sold food for customers or charities.
20. Let food banks purchase surplus produce at wholesale prices so fresh food does not go to waste.
21. Organize hotel and event-catering surplus deliveries to shelters, soup kitchens, and congregate meal programs.
22. Let restaurants sell surplus prepared meals at reduced prices through a branded “rescue meal” platform.
23. Equip community food pantries with refrigeration so they can accept fresh produce and prepared food.
24. Install monitored community refrigerators where residents can safely exchange unopened surplus food.
25. Provide produce and meal vouchers that let low-income households shop at discounted rescue markets.
26. Rotate pop-up surplus markets through neighborhoods with limited access to affordable fresh food.
27. Require school cafeterias to donate safe surplus meals to students, families, or local charities.
28. Mandate that catered city events and public-agency events donate unopened surplus food rather than discard it.
29. Run a same-day surplus meal delivery service powered by volunteer drivers and neighborhood pickup points.
30. Host weekly neighborhood food swaps so residents can share home-grown or surplus ingredients.
31. Use sales and weather data to help retailers forecast demand and avoid over-ordering fresh food.
32. Integrate point-of-sale systems with expiration alerts so store staff can act before products spoil.
33. Train store and kitchen staff to use first-in, first-out inventory rotation and label open products with dates.
34. Adopt uniform food date-labeling rules so workers and consumers can distinguish quality from safety.
35. Run public education campaigns explaining that “best by” dates often indicate quality rather than safety.
36. Require stores to mark down near-expiry products automatically before they become unsellable.
37. Create a discounted “rescue shelf” for produce that is imperfect, overripe, or cosmetically damaged but still edible.
38. Partner with neighborhood food banks to collect safe surplus directly from stores’ rescue shelves.
39. Give store managers checklists and simple tools for identifying which surplus foods are safe to donate.
40. Reduce delivery frequency or case sizes for slow-moving items so perishables spend less time in warehouses.
41. Offer small grocers and convenience stores grants for energy-efficient refrigerators that keep food safer longer.
42. Provide shared, solar-powered cold storage where small vendors can temporarily store rescued food.
43. Encourage produce suppliers to use breathable, moisture-conscious packaging that extends fruit and vegetable shelf life.
44. Require city departments and subsidized programs to purchase rescued produce when quality and price allow.
45. Allow restaurants to donate surplus through vetted community kitchens that handle preparation and food safety.
46. Build a shared commercial kitchen where small food businesses can process donated ingredients into meals.
47. Teach culinary students and chefs to create appealing menu items from surplus and imperfect ingredients.
48. Set smaller default entrée portions in restaurants and offer free refills for customers who need more.
49. Use smaller buffet trays and replenish them more often to keep food from sitting out and becoming waste.
50. Serve smaller children’s portions with free refills so families can finish meals without leftovers.
51. Offer half-size entrées, split dishes, and family-style options to reduce plate waste.
52. Ask customers about preferred portions through optional digital feedback forms and adjust menus accordingly.
53. Weigh food discarded at restaurant bins with calibrated scales to reveal which menu items create the most waste.
54. Display daily surplus-meal listings and discounts on restaurant apps and neighborhood noticeboards.
55. Offer customers a discount for taking home leftover portions in their own reusable containers.
56. Require restaurants to donate safe surplus food instead of sending it to landfills once it is no longer saleable.
57. Require that surplus food unsuitable for donation be separated for animal feed, rendering, or anaerobic digestion where regulations permit.
58. Give businesses practical food waste reduction guides covering storage, preparation, portioning, and donation.
59. Host “use-it-up” cooking classes that teach residents how to turn leftovers and wilting produce into complete meals.
60. Publish a free collection of leftover recipes in print, online, and at library and clinic locations.
61. Create a city-sponsored app that helps households inventory their refrigerator and freezer contents and plan meals.
62. Organize community freezer banks where residents can store abundant batches of homemade food safely.
63. Provide free refrigerator and freezer shelves so residents can store produce safely and see what they already have.
64. Run a month-long citywide challenge that rewards households for tracking and reducing their food waste.
65. Hold an annual “Biggest Saver” competition with prizes for households, schools, and restaurants.
66. Recruit neighborhood volunteers as food waste ambassadors who host local demonstrations and events.
67. Form a youth ambassador program that has students lead anti-waste campaigns in schools and neighborhoods.
68. Partner with supermarkets to let neighborhood groups collect safe surplus directly at scheduled times.
69. Offer free cooking classes for low-income families that feature inexpensive ingredients and ways to use scraps.
70. Teach residents safe freezing, pickling, dehydrating, and fermenting techniques through community workshops.
71. Distribute reusable food-storage containers, vacuum-seal bags, and freezer labels through libraries and food-assistance sites.
72. Create a lending library for equipment such as dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and canning pots.
73. Place campaign messages in utility bills, transit ads, schools, and clinics in multiple languages.
74. Install “eat it up” refrigerator reminders that remind residents to use food nearing its date.
75. Connect safe surplus foods unsuitable for human consumption with licensed animal-feed producers and rendering facilities.
76. Conduct school food waste audits so cafeteria managers can see how much students leave and why.
77. Give students digital or table-side feedback on their plate waste to encourage them to take only what they will eat.
78. Create school gardens that grow produce for cafeterias and teach students how to compost food scraps.
79. Train school food-service staff to plan production around attendance, taste preferences, and actual consumption.
80. Invite families to sample and vote on school meals to reduce rejections and plate waste.
81. Require city-funded event caterers to record leftover quantities and adjust their future orders accordingly.
82. Establish farmers market “surplus tables” where vendors can sell discounted produce at the end of the day.
83. Launch a gleaning program that sends trained volunteers to harvest and donate uncollected produce from urban gardens and orchards.
84. Help residents plant and maintain fruit trees by providing volunteer harvesting groups that will pick and donate the fruit.
85. Create a registry of community gardens so excess garden produce can be matched with pantries and soup kitchens.
86. Use city farmers markets as distribution hubs for produce rescued from grocers and gardens.
87. Organize seasonal preservation drives that teach residents to freeze, can, and dehydrate surplus produce.
88. Require large generators of food waste to submit reduction plans and report diversion volumes each quarter.
89. Launch a public dashboard that tracks food donation, compost tonnage, and landfill diversion by neighborhood and business type.
90. Set a citywide target to cut per-capita food waste within five years and review progress annually.
91. Tie municipal purchasing contracts to surplus-donation performance so large city suppliers have an incentive to divert food.
92. Offer reduced permit fees or priority permitting to businesses that donate surplus food or eliminate edible waste.
93. Partner with local utilities to fund efficient refrigeration and lighting upgrades in food rescue facilities.
94. Require food rescue organizations to maintain backup generators and emergency cold storage for heat waves and disasters.
95. Give restaurants standardized cold-chain guidance and insulated transport containers for safe surplus deliveries.
96. Train food-rescue volunteers in food safety, allergen handling, and respectful distribution practices.
97. Measure results with kitchen-scale audits and waste characterization studies at the household, restaurant, and retail levels.
98. Include food waste reduction in the city’s climate and resilience plan alongside methane and landfill goals.
99. Ensure surplus food programs serve rural, low-income, and culturally diverse neighborhoods rather than concentrating in affluent areas.
100. Create a cross-department food waste task force with residents, businesses, nonprofits, and waste haulers to coordinate action.

64. Provide reusable, standardized donation bins that businesses exchange for empty ones on pickup.
65. Create a "Waste-Smart Partner" certification for businesses that meet reduction and donation targets.
66. Offer grants to restaurants for forecasting software, smaller dishware, and donation refrigeration.
67. Launch a curbside "fridge emergency" service for residents whose power fails and food spoils.
68. Create a "waste-free events" permit program guiding festival organizers to donate leftovers and use reusable dishware.

73. Build an app that shows which neighborhood pantries need specific food items most urgently.

77. Put food-waste data on the city's open-data portal so residents and researchers can track it.
78. Commission a university partnership to conduct a citywide food-waste audit every two years.
79. Weigh food waste at selected businesses and curbside routes to improve forecasts and verify progress.
80. Give households easy-to-use kitchen scales and apps that estimate how much food they discard and where savings are possible.
81. Run a citywide "Waste Less, Feed More" pledge for businesses, schools, and households.
82. Encourage donation before composting by giving donors clear rules and liability protection.
83. Publish a directory of donation organizations with current pickup schedules and contact details.
84. Coordinate food-rescue work with existing mutual-aid and disaster-relief groups to avoid duplication.
85. Site rescue hubs at large food warehouses to sort donations before they reach pantries.
86. Equip food pantries with digital inventory tools so they can accept and move fresh surplus quickly.
87. Host seasonal Preservation Fairs where experts teach residents how to store and preserve peak produce.
88. Coordinate with schools, leagues, and arenas to donate surplus concession food after events.
89. Support upcycling businesses that turn surplus food into sauces, soups, snacks, and beverages.
90. Offer incentives for farmers to donate or process surplus rather than abandon it in fields.
91. Partner with rendering and biodiesel programs to collect restaurant cooking oil and fats.
92. Provide businesses with waste-tracking logs and simple software to record why food is discarded and track monthly trends.
93. Offer repair and maintenance programs for household refrigerators and freezers to prevent spoilage.
94. Offer meal-planning workshops for families facing time and budget constraints.
95. Provide starter kits with recipe cards, storage containers, and freezer bags to households receiving food assistance.
96. Staff a city hotline where residents can report illegal dumping and request collection help.
97. Create a "Fridge Share" network where restaurants list daily surplus on public boards outside their doors.
98. Encourage employers to include food-waste reduction in staff wellness and sustainability programs.
99. Include food-waste targets in city purchasing contracts for school, hospital, and employee catering.
100. Publish an annual city food-waste report that celebrates progress and sets goals for the following year.

lists.text:
1. Conduct a citywide food-waste audit to establish how much food is discarded by households, restaurants, grocers, and institutions.
2. Set a multiyear food-waste reduction goal with annual targets for households, businesses, and public institutions.
3. Require large food generators to record discarded food by type and report it annually.
4. Phase in curbside collection of food scraps separately from regular trash.
5. Offer households a lower trash rate when they use a food-scrap collection service.
6. Require large supermarkets and caterers to have written plans for donating edible surplus food.
7. Offer tax credits for businesses that document food-waste prevention and donation expenses.
8. Adopt a disposal fee that increases with the volume of food waste sent to landfills or incinerators.
9. Create a municipal surplus-food directory connecting food producers with food banks, shelters, and community groups.
10. Provide matching grants to small restaurants for waste-tracking equipment, safe storage, and compact freezers.
11. Help neighborhood grocery stores obtain food-safe handling, refrigeration, and cold-storage equipment.
12. Establish food-rescue agreements between food banks and local retailers, hotels, bakeries, and caterers.
13. Protect food donors from unnecessary liability through clear city guidance and model agreements.
14. Ban intentional destruction of edible food while allowing documented donations, animal feed, or composting.
15. Require city-funded events to plan quantities carefully and donate unopened surplus food.
16. Train grocery managers to forecast demand using sales history, weather, holidays, and local events.
17. Use automatic markdowns to move products nearing their sell-by date before they spoil.
18. Set maximum display times for highly perishable bakery and prepared-food items so stores act before quality declines.
19. Install self-service produce scales that automatically apply end-of-day discounts to weighed surplus items.
20. Build a shared exchange where nearby stores can transfer safe surplus inventory before it expires.
21. Install shelf-life alerts that flag products likely to spoil before normal stock rotation.
22. Require first-expiring-first-out procedures in grocery coolers and storage rooms.
23. Improve receiving procedures so damaged products are identified and redirected before their quality declines.
24. Create preordered bags of cosmetically imperfect produce sold through neighborhood pickup points.
25. Offer produce in smaller package sizes and flexible quantities suited to different household sizes.
26. Expand frozen and preserved-food options to help shoppers use seasonal purchases before they perish.
27. Coordinate store orders with actual sell-through data to reduce over-ordering and excess inventory.
28. Improve staff scheduling and rapid-response purchasing so demand spikes do not lead to overproduction.
29. Equip store back rooms with waste scales and simple tracking sheets to reveal recurring loss problems.
30. Provide retailers with staff training on safe handling, donation, animal-feed options, and waste prevention.
31. Create a local certification program for retailers that consistently reduce and donate surplus food.
32. Require food retailers to provide convenient collection bins for customers bringing their own containers.
33. Use reusable shipping crates for local produce distributors to reduce bruising and spoilage.
34. Require commercial waste-hauling contracts to include separate food-scrap collection service.
35. Establish a central redistribution warehouse that moves safe surplus from small stores to food banks and community kitchens.
36. Organize collective purchasing and shared storage among small grocers to reduce overstock.
37. Provide recipe cards and short videos showing shoppers how to cook products at peak ripeness.
38. Run in-store campaigns that place highly perishable products at the front of displays and in meal-kit bundles.
39. Partner with local farms to sell surplus produce through neighborhood markets at reduced prices.
40. Offer retailers lower waste-disposal fees when they document donations of edible inventory.
41. Teach residents through schools, libraries, and utility bills how to plan meals and use leftovers.
42. Offer free household food-planning classes at community centers and libraries.
43. Promote shopping with a written list through grocery-store signage and neighborhood campaigns.
44. Encourage residents to photograph and share their refrigerator inventories before shopping.
45. Create a city app that suggests recipes based on foods residents need to use first.
46. Place clearly labeled “eat first” bins and shelves in community centers, workplaces, and schools.
47. Teach residents to label homemade leftovers with dates and consume them within safe time limits.
48. Distribute refrigerator-storage guides showing how to keep produce, meat, dairy, and bread fresh longer.
49. Encourage families to freeze bread, meat, cheese, and ripe produce before they spoil.
50. Recommend buying frozen foods, loose produce, and only package sizes households will finish.
51. Run cooking demonstrations focused on turning leftover ingredients into soups, stocks, sauces, and snacks.
52. Support neighborhood food-sharing cupboards where residents can leave unwanted unopened food.
53. Launch a citywide app for reporting unwanted unopened food and arranging same-day pickup.
54. Partner with apartment managers to place food-scrap bins near mailrooms, laundry rooms, and shared kitchens.
55. Install public compost stations at farmers markets, parks, and community gardens.
56. Provide free home compost bins and starter kits to households that cannot use curbside collection.
57. Teach residents safe pickling, drying, and canning through hands-on community-kitchen workshops.
58. Explain the difference between quality dates and strict safety dates through labels, signage, and educational materials.
59. Encourage restaurants to offer half portions, split entrées, and smaller side dishes.
60. Run campaigns that promote taking leftovers for lunch and freezing them for later meals.
61. Require restaurants to record and review food waste before and after customer service.
62. Give restaurant staff short training in portion control, forecasting, safe donation, and leftover handling.
63. Organize daily collection routes for cafes and bakeries to donate safe unsold bread and pastries.
64. Equip food banks and shelters with refrigerated storage for regular surplus-food deliveries.
65. Create a municipal kitchen that transforms surplus produce into meals for community programs.
66. Offer low-interest loans to food banks and community groups that purchase discounted surplus food for distribution.
67. Require hotels to donate unopened breakfast items and surplus banquet food.
68. Establish shared kitchens where caterers and small producers can process surplus food safely.
69. Require large caterers and event organizers to submit surplus-food reports and improvement plans.
70. Host quarterly surplus-food collection days with clear safety rules and scheduled pickup slots.
71. Give food trucks and street vendors access to a shared real-time inventory platform to reduce overproduction.
72. Create a shared freezer network so businesses can preserve surplus ingredients without buying expensive equipment.
73. Let restaurants pre-sell surplus meals at a discount before closing so buyers can collect them promptly.
74. Help schools, hospitals, and other institutions reduce tray and production waste through better demand forecasting.
75. Partner with universities to evaluate local food-waste interventions and publish the findings openly.
76. Work with local utilities to distribute food-waste tips on bills and through customer accounts.
77. Form a food-waste task force involving city departments, businesses, nonprofits, and residents.
78. Give recognition and small grants to neighborhoods that achieve measurable food-waste reductions.
79. Run an annual citywide food-waste challenge with prizes for households and businesses.
80. Launch multilingual campaigns showing the financial and environmental savings from preventing food waste.
81. Require new apartment buildings to include dedicated, ventilated food-scrap rooms and convenient resident access.
82. Equip institutional kitchens with scales and waste stations to measure and categorize discarded food.
83. Create a shared dashboard that tracks food-waste trends while protecting confidential business information.
84. Use route-optimization software to improve the efficiency of surplus-food pickups and food-scrap collections.
85. Standardize business bins and signs that clearly separate donation, animal-feed, and composting streams.
86. Establish local rules for sending clean food scraps to licensed livestock-feed operations where appropriate.
87. Build partnerships with regional farms to divert unavoidable produce trimmings into animal feed or compost.
88. Develop a regional composting or anaerobic-digestion facility for unavoidable food scraps that cannot be donated.
89. Measure methane generated by discarded food to assess whether diversion projects deliver climate benefits.
90. Help restaurants redesign menus to use more of each ingredient and reduce preparation waste.
91. Encourage restaurants to buy adaptively and feature surplus produce in daily specials.
92. Train food-service staff to separate edible trimmings from plate waste to improve donation and recovery.
93. Offer curbside pickup for residents’ unwanted unopened food during designated weekly collection windows.
94. Coordinate food-rescue pickups with regular waste-collection schedules to reduce transportation energy.
95. Adopt purchasing standards that make it easy for city departments to donate unopened food.
96. Require large events to provide donation stations for safe surplus food and reusable takeout containers.
97. Reduce food-service waste in municipal buildings through smaller buffet trays, preordered meals, and careful forecasting.
98. Include food-waste data in the city’s annual sustainability report and budget review.
99. Review municipal food-waste policies every two years and adjust them based on measured results.
100. Fund a dedicated food-waste coordinator to connect city programs, businesses, donors, and recipients.
